 US News Agregar Clarín en X How to refinance student loans?
 Refinancing can lower your rate and monthly payment on student loans.
 Moving federal loans to a private lender means losing forgiveness and income-driven repayment.
 How to refinance student loans?
 NEWSROOM CLARIN Millions of Americans carrying student loans are looking for ways to shrink their monthly bills, and refinancing is one of the most common options. The process replaces your existing loans with a single new private loan, ideally with a lower interest rate or better terms.
 The stakes are high. The average borrower leaves school with $39,075 in student loan deb t, while graduate students owe roughly $106,129 on average, according to the Education Data Initiative.
 Timing matters, too. A federal appeals court approved the Education Department's settlement of a 2024 lawsuit, officially ending the SAVE repayment plan and forcing about 7 million enrolled borrowers into a different program. Many of them are now reviewing their options.
 Should you refinance your student loans?. REUTERS/Elizabeth Frantz But refinancing isn't for everyone. Moving federal loans to a private lender means giving up federal protections such as income-driven repayment, forgiveness programs, deferment and forbearance.
 Should you refinance your student loans?
 Start by figuring out whether you hold federal or private loans, or a mix of both. Federal loans are backed by the Education Department and are requested through the FAFSA, while private loans come from banks, credit unions or online lenders. Both types can be refinanced, but only through a private lender.
 If you're working toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness or the Teacher Loan Forgiveness Program, or you depend on an income-driven plan, refinancing federal loans could cost you more than it saves.
 Should you refinance your student loans?. If your main goal is a single monthly payment, a Direct Consolidation Loan from the government lets you keep federal benefits. Your rate won't necessarily drop, though, and NEA Member Benefits warns that consolidating restarts the 10-year clock for borrowers on track for PSLF.
 Steps to refinance student loans
 Once you decide to move forward, the refinancing process generally looks like this:
 Gather your financial information. Have your income, total student loan debt and an estimate of your credit score ready.
 Compare lenders. Look at rates, terms, origination fees and prepayment penalties. Prequalifying usually involves a soft credit check that shouldn't affect your score, but confirm that with the lender.
 Choose a loan. The lowest rate isn't always the cheapest option overall, since a longer term or an origination fee can raise your total cost.
 Collect your documents . Lenders may ask for proof of citizenship, your Social Security number, paystubs or tax returns, and statements for the loans you want to refinance.
 Apply . The lender will typically run a hard credit inquiry, which usually lowers your score by five points or less for a limited time.
 Wait for approval. It can take anywhere from 24 hours to a couple of weeks. Keep paying your old loans until you get confirmation they've been paid off.
 What lenders look for
 Lenders set your rate based on your credit score, income, payment history and debt-to-income ratio. Brian Reed, head of partnerships and business development at College Ave, told NEA Member Benefits that a borrower's DTI typically must be below 50% and that a FICO score in at least the upper 600s is required.
 College Ave also requires that your student loans total between $5,000 and $150,000, or up to $300,000 for borrowers with medical or veterinary degrees , and that you've graduated from a degree-granting school. Other lenders set their own criteria.
 What lenders look for. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP) If your credit falls short, adding a creditworthy cosigner may help you qualify. Just remember that person becomes responsible for the debt if you stop paying.
 Fixed vs. variable rates and loan terms
 The length of your repayment term is a key trade-off. "The longer the term, the lower the monthly payments will be," said Brian Walsh, head of advice and planning at SoFi, but you'll pay more interest over the life of the loan.
 You'll also choose between a fixed rate , which stays the same, and a variable rate, which may start lower but can rise over time. Many lenders also offer a 0.25% rate discount for enrolling in autopay.
